Life knows nothing about years, as Bukowski said; for I live through this massive weight while still only eighteen, carrying a broken body and a pain akin to a lifelong hemorrhage from a wound whose cause, extent, or cure I never understood. Living through deep, enduring turmoil often ended in numbness or detachment from that unseen, festering wound that still bleeds. The blood flowing from it endlessly was like that of a patient exhausted by a senseless illness, his fear, and the changing moods of doctors, or like a soldier trapped in a battle from which he cannot withdraw, knowing neither his role nor its eventual end... this blood is the ink with which my life, every step, and my ruin were written. Others exploited this bleeding from the living, or were too blind to see the human behind it, seeing nothing in me other than this pain, using it to feed my decay and exhaustion until I was largely destroyed, sometimes finding nothing else left.
And my mind still drowning within this narrow skull, the terrifying world, the triviality of reality, and all those frightening probabilities that have grown as close as breath—no longer mere probabilities, but a slow, unfolding reality.
Yet I destroyed myself with love, with purity, and by failing to hate my mother, to distance myself from her, or to be harsh with her even by accepting her truth—she and everyone like her who contributed to destroying me, losing me, and draining what remained of me. My purity is what polluted me, my sensitive awareness is what made me fragile, and my love for others is what made me their prey. Yet let there be no mistake: I was never weak, nor was I ever incapable of striking back, of being callous, of manipulating others, of entering into interest-based relationships without the slightest care, of selling myself physically, or of living comfortably at others' expense—whether back in the debris of past years, during the height of my illness, or afterward. I was prey by circumstance, but I possessed a sharp, intelligent predator's mind, fully aware of the world's malice and how easily I could have turned into a genuinely harsh person, utilizing whatever cunning at my disposal. Yet, this awareness did not push me toward malice; I simply refused to be polluted by hatred, even though it dwelt within me and weighed on my peace, choosing not to be harmful despite harsh realities and circumstances that left me with no other way.
And my attempts to live drained me further because I genuinely wanted to live, rather than consuming myself in the trivialities of ordinary life, or becoming like my mother—a mother whose existence I never truly recognized—or fading away like the doctor who destroyed me. Now I have reached a stage where I stand suddenly before death, disability, or irreversible loss—the result of countless circumstances beyond my control, a childhood suffering that left me with no innocence, no space even for a room, no safety, and no truth, claiming my body now, the future, and even the love that led me here, which was the true wound, the hemorrhage, and the decay I became.
When I tried to share tea with my mother recently to partake in her company and return to picking at my wound through her, I found nothing but decay filling my eyes, my stomach, and my senses completely. At that moment I realized my death, my pain, and that I have become permanently deformed—distorted by human hands and forced into this ruin against my will—even though I still possess the heart and features of a child, and still lack the strength even to hate the doctor who destroyed me without justification, or to hate her, or others like me who accompanied me on the train of my life, or to protect myself from her because I see that as cruelty toward her and her destruction of me, so as not to hurt her with a word that will never affect her in the least, such as my death.
The cup in my hand trembled along with my eyes, and the tremor of my frail body increased as I looked at her... she hurt me, and I felt a genuine fear that she sees me and I mean nothing to her, and she never allowed me to find my way to knowing this, nor to liberate myself from it, nor did she ever show me any pity, or even a shred of honesty, even after my distortion—while I was still waiting for her to offer me that. Now she no longer carries this wound, nor the hemorrhage, nor that presence... I realized that she ended herself from the moment of my birth wound, even though she exists completely, and that I am the one who has been ending ever since through my very existence.

I withdrew from her company with the tea cup in my hand—which only worsened my health, throwing my body into severe turmoil, making my heart pound fiercely, intensifying my disorientation, and leaving me feeling like an alien, isolated creature—and went to my room, which for the first time has become a room of my own. But this happened only after I lost myself and was finally able to decide to accept my death alone, to continue without resistance, to pity myself a little for living, loving, and bleeding, to let the wound bleed in peace, to let my body reach its end, and to forget the noise of reality for a little while so I could return and listen inwardly to Mahler’s Adagietto, which I used to listen to for long hours at the beginning of my adolescence, the peak of my life, or the turmoil of my wound.
I know my essence is something other than my reality, yet I accept reality, recognizing that this bodily disability, the pain, the distortions, and everything that ended in decay is not me, but is inside me, becoming a part of me as I end within it. We must not always resist; sometimes, resistance in its usual form becomes suicide or foolishness. There are things from which there is no escape, no happy endings, no ideal reality, and nothing entirely pure. Yet beauty lies in our ability to remain ourselves, despite all wounds, distortions, and even decay, passing through bleeding, destruction, and death without losing something deep inside—even if it were a piece by Mahler or some other good music, which continues to give a sense of existence despite everything, enough peace to accept reality, and something of the memory of nostalgia or a once-real beauty. I wept a lot while listening to this music; it was wonderful! I found myself feeling a profound nostalgia even for the most tragic things in my life: for my childhood and the doll I left behind when a genocide struck, back when I was six, weeping because I thought she would be killed; for the people who hurt me, including those who still do, yet whom I truly love, my family, and all those old memories, both beautiful and harsh; even for my doctor who completely destroyed my nervous system, and my old friend who was that deep breach tearing away a piece of me, becoming a gateway for every love, pain, and loss in this childlike heart, stripping away my remaining barriers and leaving me utterly weakened to face the harshest circumstances. And for all those influential writers I can no longer read because it pains me so much to realize how much I miss them, most notably Bukowski. Illness has even robbed me of the ability to die, but I was able to cry, to remember, and to return to myself for a little while before exhaustion, distraction, and chronic pain took over again.
Amidst all this, I found myself returning to an old childhood habit, sucking my thumb just as I used to do back then, trying to soothe my agony because it was the only thing left that could offer me comfort, make me feel safe and alive, with no other painkiller left in this world. I live while exhausting myself so as not to go mad from the terror, trying to protect myself every single time before this frail structure is completely destroyed—while, every now and then, encountering some glimpse of beauty, even if only in my imagination.
And yet, not long ago, someone appeared in my life—someone who was meant to be just a friend, whom I met while he was troubled, going through a hard time. I was simply present, listening and sharing long conversations around his endless problems, investing energy and health from a body already exhausted, simply because I am as bold in love as others are in hatred, refusing to let myself be polluted by it, even as that hatred stored its poison within my suffering, my body, and even my sleep. My role remained confined to listening and supporting, while he never bothered to ask how I was doing. He did not know that I suffer from a chronic disease devouring my body thanks to doctors who harmed me and caused this condition; he did not know that I live in fear of returning to the old exile, or of my family's deterioration while I struggle alone—despite everything—trying to save them while they are entirely helpless. He did not know that when I gave him my time and attention, it was not to ask for anything in return, but because I wanted to offer him a glimpse of my humanity and a sense of shared human kinship so he wouldn’t feel alone, carving out a genuine piece of my drained health from amidst difficult circumstances. He did not know that I am a person deeply suppressed and unable to feel, unable even to weep to release my pain, and whose health collapses from any human interaction or emotional friction; a person living with a fractured mind and chronic pain, sometimes unable to even bathe from sheer helplessness, and unable to sleep like normal human beings except in brief, broken, nightmare-filled fragments. And when I felt my life was once again threatened by destruction—facing the specter of exile and the crumbling of my attempts to save my family while they remained helpless—I wept and screamed. I became like a quiet, agonizing self-destruction moving on all fronts, with a sharp tongue and an elegant facade, pleading with the phantom of my doctor, wishing he had at least left me the choice of death, life, or sleep. And when my phone broke amidst that screaming and emotional breakdown—destroying the remnants of my health so I wouldn't direct it at anyone, relapse into suicide, or plan to sell myself—I understood the true meaning of fear, lost my final link to humanity, and realized I was in hell.
I never wanted anything from him except mercy, or simply to be left alone—not to be treated like a passing toy that others step past, recoiling in aversion from my pain without even trying to understand my reality, just as happened with this person. And when I realized all of this, beyond just his disappointment, I understood a deeper, harsher truth: that my self-destruction, or even pushing myself to the brink of ruin through trying with others while caring little for my own life, does not stop with me alone; my collapse inevitably pulls others down into ruin with it. My destruction means the destruction of others, and since I never wanted to hurt anyone, I realized how deeply interconnected this is—meaning that even my silence and self-preservation are part of my desire not to be the cause of anyone's harm. Yet he turned out to be just another person who manipulated, pressured, and tried to completely exploit and drain someone like me, lying continuously until it reached the point where he attempted to exploit me sexually, then denied it and played games. What he did was more than enough to completely break me down. And now, having lost even my capacity to try or risk, I had to pull away entirely, remaining silent, showing nothing, needing nothing more than to buy a lock for my room door, fix my phone, and be left alone to die in my place, while caring for my little birds.
I think my chances are running out. When my health deteriorates in medical settings that fail to understand my condition—because it is chronic and advanced, yet shows nothing in lab tests while I outwardly appear resilient—it invites failed medical attempts that destroy me even further, a hidden destruction that leaves no trace on tests. This threatens to drag me toward an asylum where my suffering is misunderstood as mere madness, or trap me in an unlivable hell of chronic pain, neurological collapse, and the loss of my mind, or leave me bedridden. All these terrifying probabilities point to a slow death where I cannot protect myself, losing all elements of life as my body is destroyed from within. Before reaching that final stage, or as part of this inescapable reality, I might even resort to suicide or some other form of complete loss. Above all else, what I want simply is never to hurt anyone. I feel trapped facing these options, knowing that in the end, much will not change—it is simply a matter of time, and I am trying to accept it, while I still listen to the music, love my little birds, and try to possess enough dignity to bathe alone, not to be humiliated any further, and to keep the remnants of my health from being ruined, wishing that as I take my final breath, I could once again hold that small cat I had hugged on the street a while ago before it disappeared—remembering that astonishing warmth which overflowed with the pure spirit of childhood—a warmth that was enough on its own to make me endure the thought of tomorrow, the chronic pain, all the terrifying possibilities, the harshness of reality, the constant threat under which I live, and the utter isolation. It was then I realized that this bleeding would never truly cease except through my own death, and I became able to listen to the dripping of my own blood without fear, and to breathe through my wound without hiding it, wishing only that, with my final breath, I could once again hold that very cat to reclaim everything the world stripped away from me.
